## Three-field rotation `three_field_system`
- Deps: helped by heavy_plough, horse_collar_harness, legumes_green_manure
- Core idea: Divide the arable land into three parts: one sown in autumn with wheat or rye, one sown in spring with oats, barley, peas or beans, one left fallow and grazed; rotate every year. Compared with the two-field system (half the land fallow) two thirds of the land bear a crop each year, the work and the harvest risk are spread over two seasons, and the spring field gives oats for horses and legumes that restore the soil. It needs enough summer rain for spring crops, so it suits northern Europe better than the dry Mediterranean.
- Pitfalls: Expecting it to work in dry-summer climates such as Tuscany or Greece, where spring-sown crops fail and two-field rotation persisted for good reason | Thinking the fallow is idle land: it is ploughed several times to kill weeds and is manured by grazing stock | Forgetting that open-field villages rotate in common; one farmer cannot change the system alone | Claiming a sudden Carolingian 'invention'; the spread was slow and regional (8th to 13th century)
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – two-field rotation with fallow is the Mediterranean norm (Columella, Pliny); europe: late 8th c. – White dates early documentary evidence from Carolingian lands to 763; the timing of adoption on individual estates is less certain; general in northern Europe only by the 12th–13th c.; china: by 6th c. AD – multi-year rotations of cereals and legumes without fallow described in the Qimin yaoshu
- Read: Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962) | Adriaan Verhulst, The Carolingian Economy (2002) | Georges Duby, Rural Economy and Country Life in the Medieval West (1968)

## Legumes and green manure `legumes_green_manure`
- Deps: helped by nitrogen_fixation_biology
- Core idea: Peas, beans, vetch, lupins, clover and lucerne (alfalfa) enrich the soil instead of exhausting it, because bacteria in the nodules on their roots take nitrogen from the air. Grow a legume before a cereal, or sow it and plough it in green before it sets seed (green manure); the following grain crop yields markedly more. Clover and lucerne also give the best hay, so more animals and more dung. Demonstration: two strips side by side, one after beans or clover, one after grain, both then sown with wheat.
- Pitfalls: Saying legumes 'draw fertility from the deep soil'; the gain is nitrogen from the air, fixed in the root nodules | Harvesting the whole plant, roots and all, and expecting the full benefit; most of the nitrogen leaves with the seed and hay unless residues or dung return to the field | Sowing clover too often on the same land (clover sickness); leave at least four to six years between clover crops | Expecting legumes to replace phosphate, potash or lime; on sour soil clover hardly grows at all
- History: mesopotamia: c. 8000–7000 BC – lentil, pea, chickpea and bitter vetch among the founder crops of the Fertile Crescent; china: 1st c. BC – Fan Shengzhi shu recommends beans; c. 540 AD Qimin yaoshu ranks green manures (mung bean first) and describes ploughing them in; rome: c. 160 BC – Cato lists lupins, beans and vetch as crops that manure the land; 1st c. AD Columella describes ploughing in lupins; americas: by c. 1000 BC – beans grown with maize in Mesoamerica; islamic: 10th–12th c. – lucerne (alfalfa) fodder growing in al-Andalus (Ibn al-Awwam); europe: 16th c. – sown clover in Lombardy and Flanders (Tarello, Ricordo d'agricoltura, 1567); 1838 Boussingault shows legumes gain nitrogen; 1886–88 Hellriegel and Wilfarth trace it to root-nodule bacteria
- Read: Columella, De re rustica II.10–15 | Mauro Ambrosoli, The Wild and the Sown: Botany and Agriculture in Western Europe, 1350–1850 (1997) | Francesca Bray, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 6 part 2: Agriculture (1984)

## Four-course rotation with clover and turnips `crop_rotation`
- Deps: needs legumes_green_manure; helped by seed_drill, selective_breeding, nitrogen_fixation_biology
- Core idea: Replace the fallow year with fodder crops: wheat, then turnips, then barley undersown with clover, then a year of clover (the Norfolk four-course). Turnips grown in rows are hoed, which cleans the land of weeds as a fallow would, and feed sheep and cattle through the winter; clover fixes nitrogen and gives hay. More fodder means more animals, more dung and therefore more grain from the same land, with no field ever idle. It needs enclosed or commonly agreed fields, because stock grazing the stubble would eat the clover and turnips.
- Pitfalls: Crediting 'Turnip' Townshend or Jethro Tull with inventing it; it grew out of Flemish practice over two centuries | Trying it on an open common field without agreement on grazing rights | Expecting results in one season; soil nitrogen and herds build up over several rotations | Turnips on heavy wet clay or in hot dry summers (they fail); in the south use lucerne, sainfoin or beans instead | Clover returning every fourth year for decades leads to clover sickness; vary the legume
- History: rome: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – cereal and legume alternation recommended (Virgil, Georgics I; Columella); china: c. 540 AD – Qimin yaoshu gives rotation tables of cereals, legumes and vegetables; europe: 14th–16th c. – fodder crops replace fallow in Flanders and Brabant; 1650 Richard Weston describes it for English readers; early 18th c. Norfolk four-course; general in England c. 1750–1850
- Read: Richard Weston, A Discours of Husbandrie Used in Brabant and Flanders (1650) | Mark Overton, Agricultural Revolution in England: The Transformation of the Agrarian Economy 1500–1850 (1996)

## Manure, compost and night soil `manure_compost_night_soil`
- Deps: helped by sanitation_sewerage, contagion_theory
- Core idea: What a harvest takes from the soil must be returned. Collect animal dung with the urine-soaked straw, kitchen and crop waste, pile them moist and airy in heaps of at least a cubic metre, mixing strawy (carbon-rich) with wet green or dung (nitrogen-rich) material, and turn the heap; it heats to 55–65 °C, which kills most parasites and weed seeds, and becomes dark crumbly compost in a few months. Keep the heap covered or on a hard floor so rain does not wash the goodness away. Human excreta need separate treatment that destroys persistent worm eggs throughout the material. A warm centre or a crumbly appearance cannot verify this.
- Pitfalls: Spreading fresh human excrement on vegetables that are eaten raw; this spreads worms, typhoid, cholera and dysentery | A heap that is too wet and airless rots cold and stinking and loses its nitrogen | Leaving dung in the rain and sun for months; most of the nitrogen and potash is lost | Thinking wood ash and dung are the same thing; ash gives potash and lime but no nitrogen, and mixed with fresh dung it drives ammonia off
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – manuring of fields inferred from sherd scatters around Near Eastern towns; china: by c. 3rd c. BC – systematic collection of human and animal waste; 1149 Chen Fu's Nongshu describes compost houses and 'the soil can be kept ever new'; rome: c. 160 BC – Cato on dung heaps; 1st c. AD Columella ranks dungs (pigeon first) and describes covered pits; islamic: 12th c. – Ibn al-Awwam (Seville) devotes a book to manures and composts; americas: pre-Columbian – Amazonian terra preta (charcoal, refuse and bone); guano and fish on the Peruvian coast; europe: medieval – town dung sold to gardens; Flanders famous for urban night soil by the 16th c.; 1840 Liebig's mineral theory explains what manure supplies
- Read: F. H. King, Farmers of Forty Centuries (1911) | Columella, De re rustica II.14 | Francesca Bray, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 6 part 2: Agriculture (1984)

## Liming and marling of sour soils `liming_marling`
- Deps: helped by lime_burning, acids_bases_ph
- Core idea: Rain-washed, sandy and heath soils turn sour (acid): sorrel, heather and moss thrive, clover and barley fail. Spreading ground chalk, limestone, marl (limy clay) or slaked lime, a few tonnes per hectare every several years, neutralises the acid, lets clover and beans grow and makes dung work better. Test the material: real marl or chalk fizzes in strong vinegar.
- Pitfalls: Treating lime as a fertiliser; it unlocks nutrients but supplies almost none, hence 'lime and lime without manure makes both farm and farmer poor' | Liming soil that is already chalky, which locks up iron and manganese and harms the crop | Mixing quicklime or fresh slaked lime with dung, which drives the nitrogen off as ammonia | Handling quicklime carelessly; it burns skin and eyes and heats violently with water
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny describes marling by the Gauls and Britons, with different marls for different soils (Natural History XVII); Varro saw it on the Rhine; europe: 13th c. – marl pits common in England and northern France; 18th c. liming general with cheap coal-burnt lime; 1909 Sørensen defines pH; china: by Song – lime applied to acid paddy soils in the south
- Read: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia XVII.42–48 | E. John Russell, Soil Conditions and Plant Growth (1912)

## Mineral fertiliser (guano, phosphate, potash, nitrate) `mineral_fertiliser`
- Deps: helped by sulphuric_acid, photosynthesis_plant_nutrition, ammonia_synthesis
- Core idea: Plants build their bodies from air and water but need a few mineral nutrients from the soil, above all nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; the scarcest one limits the yield (law of the minimum). These can be supplied from outside the farm: nitrogen from seabird guano or Chilean nitrate, phosphorus from bones or rock phosphate made soluble with sulphuric acid (superphosphate, roughly equal weights of ground bone or rock and acid), potassium from wood ash or potash salts. Demonstration: plots with and without each nutrient, as at Rothamsted.
- Pitfalls: Liebig's own error: he thought plants get enough nitrogen from the air and only minerals need replacing; cereals need added nitrogen | Overdosing: too much nitrogen makes cereals fall over (lodging) and scorches seedlings | Believing that humus is the food of plants (the old humus theory) | Using raw ground rock phosphate on neutral or limy soil; it is almost insoluble until treated with acid | Forgetting that guano and nitrate deposits are finite; Peru's guano was largely exhausted within forty years
- History: americas: pre-Columbian – coastal Peruvians and the Inca manure with seabird guano and protect the bird islands; 1830s Chilean nitrate exported; china: by Ming – bone ash, oil-seed cakes and lime sold as fertilisers; europe: 1804 Humboldt brings guano samples; 1828 Sprengel and 1840 Liebig state the mineral theory; 1842 Lawes patents superphosphate; 1843 Rothamsted experiments begin; 1840s guano boom; 1861 Stassfurt potash mined; 1913 synthetic ammonia
- Read: Justus Liebig, Organic Chemistry in its Applications to Agriculture and Physiology (1840) | Gregory T. Cushman, Guano and the Opening of the Pacific World (2013) | Vaclav Smil, Enriching the Earth (2001)

## Terracing and soil conservation `terracing_soil_conservation`
- Deps: helped by surveying_triangulation
- Core idea: Ploughed soil on a slope washes away far faster than nature makes it (about a millimetre a year lost against a few hundredths formed), so hill farming ruins itself within generations unless the slope is broken. Build dry-stone walls along the contour, leaning slightly into the hill, fill behind with rubble for drainage and soil on top, and lead surplus water off in lined channels. Where there are no terraces, plough along the contour, keep the ground covered and leave the steepest land in wood or pasture.
- Pitfalls: Ploughing straight up and down the slope, which turns every furrow into a gully | Building terraces and then not maintaining them; one burst wall takes the ones below with it | Clearing the forest on the hills above a town and being surprised by floods and silted harbours | Walls without drainage; the trapped water pushes them over
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3000 BC – Bronze Age terraces in the Levant and Yemen highlands (dates approximate); americas: from c. 2000 BC in the Andes; 15th c. Inca state terraces with stone-lined drains (Pisac, Moray); 1935 the United States establishes the Soil Conservation Service after severe erosion; china: terraced fields named (titian) in 12th-c. texts; loess and southern rice terraces older; east_asia: Ifugao rice terraces (Philippines) – traditionally 2,000 years old; recent archaeology suggests after c. 1600 (disputed); greece: 4th c. BC – Plato (Critias 111) describes Attica's hills as stripped of soil; europe: medieval and early modern – Mediterranean terraces for vines and olives
- Read: David R. Montgomery, Dirt: The Erosion of Civilizations (2007) | R. A. Donkin, Agricultural Terracing in the Aboriginal New World (1979)

## Heavy mouldboard plough `heavy_plough`
- Deps: helped by bloomery_iron, horse_collar_harness, blast_furnace_cast_iron
- Core idea: Three working parts on a strong frame: an iron knife (coulter) cuts the sod vertically, an iron share cuts it horizontally, and a curved board (mouldboard) behind the share turns the slice over to one side, burying weeds and stubble. Unlike the light scratch plough (ard) it can work heavy wet clay in one pass and, by throwing the soil into ridges, drains it. It is hard to pull (teams of four to eight oxen in early medieval Europe) and hard to turn, so fields become long strips; a well-curved iron mouldboard, as in China, cuts the draught to one or two animals.
- Pitfalls: Recommending it for light, dry Mediterranean soils, where deep turning dries the ground and the ard is the better tool | A flat or badly shaped mouldboard that pushes soil instead of turning it and doubles the draught | Ignoring the cost of the team; peasants had to pool oxen, which shaped the whole village | Calling it a medieval invention out of nothing; Roman and Chinese precursors existed
- History: china: c. 3rd c. BC – cast-iron shares; by 1st c. BC curved cast-iron mouldboards in the Han state iron works; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny mentions a wheeled plough with coulter in Raetia (Natural History XVIII.172); europe: 6th–10th c. – heavy plough spreads on the clay lands north of the Alps (chronology disputed); 1730 Rotherham plough with curved iron-clad mouldboard, possibly after Dutch and Chinese models; americas: 1837 – John Deere makes a steel plough in Illinois; india: ards with iron shares from c. 1000 BC; mouldboard ploughs only in the colonial period
- Read: Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962) | Francesca Bray, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 6 part 2: Agriculture (1984) | Thomas B. Andersen, Peter S. Jensen & Christian V. Skovsgaard, The heavy plow and the agricultural revolution in Medieval Europe, Journal of Development Economics 118 (2016)

## Horse collar and breast-strap harness `horse_collar_harness`
- Core idea: A horse pulls best from its shoulders and chest. The collar is a rigid, padded oval frame fitted to the individual horse that rests on the shoulders and leaves the windpipe free; the traces run back from wooden or metal bars (hames) on the collar at about mid-height to a swingletree. A well-harnessed horse typically walks faster than an ox, which matters for ploughing in short weather windows and for road haulage. An ox yoke or a strap round the neck wastes much of the horse's strength.
- Pitfalls: Repeating that the ancient harness 'strangled' horses and made them nearly useless; Spruytte's reconstructions showed this was much overstated | A badly fitting collar, which galls the shoulders and lames the horse within days | Forgetting the costs: horses need oats and shoes and are worth little as meat, so oxen stayed the cheaper choice in much of Europe | Attaching the traces too high or too low, so that the collar rides up onto the throat
- History: china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – breast-strap harness; c. 5th–6th c. AD – collar harness (Dunhuang murals, as read by Needham); rome: antiquity – yoke with neck and girth straps for horses and mules; adequate for light vehicles; europe: c. 8th c. – breast-strap; c. 9th–10th c. – padded collar; horses plough commonly only from the 12th c.
- Read: Joseph Needham & Wang Ling, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965) | J. Spruytte, Early Harness Systems (1983) | John Langdon, Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation (1986)

## Seed drill `seed_drill`
- Deps: helped by gears_gear_trains
- Core idea: Instead of scattering seed by hand, a drill drops it at an even rate into straight furrows of even depth (2–5 cm) and covers it: a hopper feeds a notched or grooved roller turned by the ground wheel, which meters the seed into tubes ending just behind small coulters. This saves a third or more of the seed, gives even germination, and the straight rows can be hoed between, by hand or horse, to kill weeds. The simplest form is a funnel and tube fixed behind a light plough, fed by hand.
- Pitfalls: Tull's theory was wrong: he held that finely broken earth itself feeds plants and manure is unnecessary | Using it on a rough, stony or cloddy seedbed, where the coulters ride up and the tubes block | A metering roller that crushes or bridges the seed; each crop needs its own notch size | Expecting fast adoption; in England drills became general only a century after Tull
- History: mesopotamia: by c. 2000 BC – plough with seed funnel shown on seals; the Sumerian 'Farmer's Instructions' (c. 1700 BC) prescribe seed depth and spacing; china: c. 1st c. BC – multi-tube seed drill (lou) with iron shares, attributed to Zhao Guo (c. 85 BC); india: seed-tube ploughs traditional and old; first dates uncertain; europe: 1566 – Camillo Torello's Venetian patent; c. 1701 Jethro Tull's drill, published 1731–33; general use from the early 19th c.
- Read: Jethro Tull, The Horse-Hoeing Husbandry (1733) | Francesca Bray, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 6 part 2: Agriculture (1984)

## Scythe and grain cradle `scythe_cradle`
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron
- Core idea: A long, slightly curved blade (60–90 cm) on a shaft about as tall as the mower with two handgrips, swung in a flat arc close to the ground so that it slices rather than chops. The edge is hammered thin on a small anvil (peening) and touched up with a whetstone every few minutes. One man mows about 0.4 hectare of hay a day. With a cradle, a light frame of wooden fingers above the blade that catches the stalks and lays them in a neat row, he cuts three to four times as much grain as with a sickle.
- Pitfalls: Hacking with the point instead of sliding the whole edge through the crop | Confusing blade types: thin continental blades can be peened; thicker hardened blades are ground and whetted | Mowing dead-ripe grain, which shatters and sheds seed; scythe-cut cereals are cut a little earlier | Overlooking why the sickle lasted: it allowed selective cutting of ripe heads and suited small plots; a cradle scythe also needed space and workers to bind the cut grain
- History: europe: c. 500–200 BC – short scythes in Celtic (La Tène) Europe; early Middle Ages – long hay scythe general; 14th–15th c. – cereals mown in Flanders (Hainault scythe); 18th–19th c. – scythe replaces sickle for grain; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny distinguishes the short Italian and the long Gallic scythe (Natural History XVIII.261); americas: c. 1780–1840 – the cradle scythe is the standard grain harvester in North America; china: sickles and a push-scythe with basket for buckwheat (Wang Zhen, Nongshu, 1313)
- Read: E. J. T. Collins, Harvest Technology and Labour Supply in Britain, 1790–1870, Economic History Review 22 (1969) | K. D. White, Agricultural Implements of the Roman World (1967)

## Mechanical reaper and threshing machine `reaper_thresher`
- Deps: helped by scythe_cradle, gears_gear_trains, blast_furnace_cast_iron
- Core idea: Reaper: a horse walks beside the standing crop and pulls a frame whose ground wheel drives, through gears and a crank, a toothed knife sliding to and fro through fixed pointed fingers; the fingers hold the stalks while the knife shears them, a turning reel pushes them onto a platform, and a man rakes them off for binding. It cuts 4–6 hectares a day against about one for a man with a cradle scythe. Thresher: a fast-turning drum with beater bars rubs the ears against a curved grating, then sieves and a crank-driven fan blow the chaff from the grain.
- Pitfalls: A knife without fixed fingers only pushes the stalks over; the cut is a scissor action | Pulling from directly in front, so the horses trample the crop; the draught must be offset | Machines that break down in the few days of harvest are worse than none; spare knives and a smith are part of the system | Ignoring the labourers who lose their winter threshing work; the Swing riots of 1830 destroyed hundreds of machines
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – vallus, an ox-pushed comb that strips the ears, on the big estates of Gaul (Pliny, Natural History XVIII.296; reliefs at Buzenol and Trier); china: by 1st c. BC–2nd c. AD – crank-driven rotary winnowing fan (Han tomb models); europe: 1786 – Andrew Meikle's threshing machine (Scotland); 1826–28 Patrick Bell's reaper; americas: 1831 – Cyrus McCormick demonstrates his reaper (patent 1834); 1833 Obed Hussey; 1836 Moore and Hascall combine harvester; 1878 Appleby twine binder
- Read: K. D. White, Roman Farming (1970) | Siegfried Giedion, Mechanization Takes Command (1948)

## Selective breeding of plants and animals `selective_breeding`
- Deps: helped by heredity_genetics
- Core idea: Offspring resemble their parents, so a breed can be shifted in a chosen direction by letting only the best individuals reproduce, generation after generation. Decide on a measurable aim (wool weight, milk, early ripening), keep written records of parents and offspring, judge a sire by the performance of his progeny rather than his looks, keep the chosen stock apart, and cull the rest. For crops, save seed from the best plants in the field, not from the heap. Bakewell changed English sheep and cattle within one lifetime this way.
- Pitfalls: Selling or eating the best animals and breeding from what is left | Believing that traits acquired in life (a docked tail, a trained skill) are inherited | Close inbreeding without culling: it fixes the wanted trait but also weakness and infertility | Selecting for appearance or a single trait; Bakewell's fat sheep had poor wool and fertility | Expecting quick results in animals with long generations
- History: mesopotamia: c. 9500–8000 BC – domestication of wheat, barley, sheep and goats; date palms hand-pollinated by c. 2000 BC; americas: c. 7000 BC – maize bred from teosinte in south-west Mexico; thousands of potato landraces in the Andes; china: silkworm, rice and goldfish varieties selected over millennia; early-ripening rices promoted under the Song; rome: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – Varro and Columella give rules for choosing rams, bulls and seed; islamic: medieval – recorded pedigrees of Arabian horses; europe: c. 1760–1795 – Robert Bakewell at Dishley (in-and-in breeding, progeny testing, ram letting); 1791 General Stud Book; 1859 Darwin builds on breeders' experience
- Read: Charles Darwin, The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication (1868) | Roger J. Wood & Vítězslav Orel, Genetic Prehistory in Selective Breeding: A Prelude to Mendel (2001)

## Grafting of fruit trees and vines `grafting_fruit_trees`
- Core idea: Apples, pears, stone fruit, citrus and vines do not come true from seed; a good variety is multiplied by joining a twig of it (scion) onto a rooted young plant of the same or a closely related kind (rootstock). Cut both cleanly so that the green layer just under the bark (cambium) of one lies against that of the other, bind tightly and seal with wax or clay against drying; do it in late winter with dormant scions, or set single buds in summer. The rootstock decides vigour and resistance to soil pests, the scion decides the fruit.
- Pitfalls: Believing any tree can be grafted on any other (ancient authors claimed vines on elms); only close relatives unite | Missing the cambium contact or letting the cut dry out before binding | Thinking the graft blends the two plants; scion and stock each keep their own nature | Planting pips of a good apple and expecting the same fruit | Moving rooted vines or soil between continents; this brought phylloxera to Europe
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1800 BC – a Mari tablet may refer to vine grafting (disputed); china: by 1st millennium BC; detailed instructions in the Qimin yaoshu (c. 540 AD); greece: c. 424 BC – mentioned in the Hippocratic 'On the Nature of the Child'; c. 300 BC Theophrastus explains it; rome: c. 160 BC – Cato gives step-by-step cleft and bud grafting (De agri cultura 40–42); europe: 1870s–1880s – European vines saved from phylloxera by grafting onto American rootstocks
- Read: Cato, De agri cultura 40–42 | Ken Mudge, Jules Janick, Steven Scofield & Eliezer E. Goldschmidt, A History of Grafting, Horticultural Reviews 35 (2009)

## Irrigation and water lifting (canal, qanat, shaduf, noria) `irrigation_water_lifting`
- Deps: helped by archimedes_screw, piston_pump, surveying_triangulation, water_wheel
- Core idea: Lead water to the fields by gravity where possible: a canal taken off a river upstream and run along the contour with a fall of only about one in a few thousand. Where water lies lower, lift it: the shaduf (a counterweighted pole with a bucket, lifts 2–3 m), the animal-driven geared pot wheel (saqiya, lifts 10 m and more), the noria (a large wheel with pots turned by the current), the screw and the chain pump. A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel (about 1 in 1,000) dug back from the fields into the foot of a hill until it taps groundwater, with a vertical shaft every 20–50 m for digging and air. Irrigated land must also be drained, or evaporating water leaves salt behind.
- Pitfalls: Irrigating without drainage: the water table rises, salt crusts the surface and wheat, then barley, fails; salinity reduced yields in parts of southern Mesopotamia; its wider historical role is debated | A canal that is too steep scours its bed, too flat silts up; levelling is the hard part | Standing water breeds malaria mosquitoes and, in Africa and Asia, the snails that carry bilharzia | Forgetting water law: upstream users can ruin downstream ones, so shares and turns must be fixed and enforced
- History: mesopotamia: c. 6000 BC – canals at Choga Mami; c. 2300 BC shaduf on an Akkadian seal; qanats in neighbouring Iran and Urartu from c. 800–700 BC; egypt: c. 3000 BC – basin irrigation with the Nile flood; shaduf by c. 1500 BC; saqiya in the 3rd–2nd c. BC; india: c. 2600 BC – wells and reservoirs of the Indus cities (Dholavira); Grand Anicut on the Kaveri, traditionally 2nd c. AD; china: 256 BC – Dujiangyan (Li Bing); 246 BC Zhengguo canal; square-pallet chain pump by the 1st–2nd c. AD; greece: 3rd c. BC – screw, force pump and compartmented wheel in Hellenistic Egypt; islamic: 8th–12th c. – qanat, noria and saqiya spread from Iran to Spain; great norias of Hama; americas: by c. 3400 BC – canals in the Zaña valley, Peru; c. 600–1450 AD Hohokam canal networks in Arizona
- Read: John Peter Oleson, Greek and Roman Mechanical Water-Lifting Devices: The History of a Technology (1984) | Thorkild Jacobsen & Robert M. Adams, Salt and Silt in Ancient Mesopotamian Agriculture, Science 128 (1958)

## Wet rice (paddy) cultivation `wet_rice_cultivation`
- Deps: helped by irrigation_water_lifting, terracing_soil_conservation
- Core idea: Rice is grown in dead-level fields enclosed by low banks and kept under 5–10 cm of water. Raise seedlings thickly in a small nursery bed for three to five weeks, then transplant them in rows about a hand's span apart into the puddled field; drain two weeks before harvest. The standing water drowns weeds, evens out temperature and carries nutrients, and organisms living in it fix nitrogen, so the same field can bear rice every year for centuries if nutrients removed at harvest are replaced. Quick-ripening varieties allow two crops a year or rice followed by wheat.
- Pitfalls: Fields that are not exactly level, so that part is dry and part drowned | Paddies close to towns: they breed malaria mosquitoes (Italian and Spanish cities banned them near the walls) | Living mainly on polished white rice, which causes beriberi; polishing removes the thiamine-rich bran and germ after the husk has been removed | Trying rice where the summer is cool or water short; it needs warmth and steady water for months
- History: china: c. 7000–5000 BC – rice domesticated on the Yangtze; c. 4000 BC paddy fields (Caoxieshan, Tianluoshan); transplanting described by the 2nd c. AD; 1012 early-ripening Champa rice distributed by Emperor Zhenzong; india: c. 2000 BC – rice farming in the Ganges plain (earlier dates debated); east_asia: c. 1000–300 BC – paddy rice reaches Korea and Japan; africa: c. 1000 BC – African rice (Oryza glaberrima) domesticated on the inland Niger; islamic: 8th–10th c. – rice spreads to Egypt, Sicily and Spain; europe: 1470s – rice fields in the Po valley (letter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza, 1475); americas: 1690s – rice in Carolina, drawing on West African growers' skills
- Read: Francesca Bray, The Rice Economies: Technology and Development in Asian Societies (1986) | Judith A. Carney, Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas (2001)

## Polders – land reclamation with dikes and wind pumps `windmill_drainage_land_reclamation`
- Deps: needs windmill; helped by archimedes_screw, surveying_triangulation
- Core idea: Surround marsh or a shallow lake with a ring dike and a ring canal, cut a grid of ditches inside, and let windmills lift the water from the ditches into the ring canal, from which it runs to river or sea through sluices at low water. A scoop wheel lifts only about 1.5 m, so deep lakes need two to four mills in series, each lifting into the basin of the next; a mill driving an Archimedes screw lifts 4–5 m. The Beemster (7,200 ha, 3.5 m below sea level) took 43 mills and four years. It requires lasting arrangements for shared maintenance; Dutch water boards collected levies for the dikes and mills.
- Pitfalls: Drained peat shrinks and oxidises: the land sinks by metres over the centuries, so drainage becomes ever harder (Holme Fen has sunk about 4 m since 1851) | One neglected stretch of dike floods everyone; without compulsory shared upkeep the polder fails | No wind, no pumping: storage basins are needed for calm, wet weeks | Draining coastal marsh without sea sluices that close at high tide
- History: china: Tang–Song – diked polder fields (weitian) in the Yangtze delta, drained by treadle chain pumps; europe: 11th–13th c. – Dutch and Flemish dikes, sluices and water boards (Rijnland charter 1255); 1407–08 first documented drainage windmills near Alkmaar; 1533 Achtermeer, first lake pumped dry; 1607–12 Beemster (Leeghwater); 1630s–1650s Vermuyden drains the English Fens; 1849–52 Haarlemmermeer drained by steam
- Read: G. P. van de Ven (ed.), Man-Made Lowlands: History of Water Management and Land Reclamation in the Netherlands (1993) | H. C. Darby, The Draining of the Fens (1940)

## Fish ponds and carp polyculture `aquaculture_fish_ponds`
- Core idea: Dig shallow ponds (1–2 m) with an inlet and a sluice at the lowest point so they can be drained completely, stock them with young carp, and manure the water so that it turns green: the fish live on the small life that grows in it. Keep separate spawning, nursery and fattening ponds, fish them out by draining in autumn every two or three years, and let the bed lie dry or crop it between. Chinese practice stocks several carps together that eat different things (grass carp cut grass, silver carp green water, bighead carp tiny animals, common carp the bottom), which multiplies the yield without feed.
- Pitfalls: Overstocking or over-manuring: on warm still nights the water loses its air and all the fish die at once | A pond that cannot be drained cannot be harvested or cleared of pike and disease | Eating freshwater fish raw; it carries liver flukes and tapeworm | Expecting sea fish such as herring or cod to live and breed in ponds
- History: egypt: c. 2000–1500 BC – tomb paintings of tilapia in garden ponds; china: 1st millennium BC – carp ponds; a short treatise is attributed to Fan Li (5th c. BC, probably written later); Tang (618–907) – polyculture of several carp species; rome: c. 95 BC – Sergius Orata's oyster beds; 1st c. BC–1st c. AD sea-water piscinae (Varro, Columella); europe: 11th–13th c. – carp ponds spread west from the Danube; 15th–16th c. great pond systems of Bohemia; 1547 Dubravius, De piscinis
- Read: Richard C. Hoffmann, Economic Development and Aquatic Ecosystems in Medieval Europe, American Historical Review 101 (1996) | Eugene K. Balon, Origin and domestication of the wild carp, Cyprinus carpio: from Roman gourmets to the swimming flowers, Aquaculture 129 (1995)

## Crops of the Americas (potato, maize and others) `new_world_crops`
- Deps: helped by world_geography, wind_systems_ocean_currents
- Core idea: Across the Atlantic grow food plants unknown in the Old World that out-yield its grains. Maize (Mexico to the Caribbean) returns 100 seeds or more for one sown, against 4–6 for European wheat. The potato (high Andes of Peru and Bolivia) gives two to three times the calories of grain per field and grows in cool, wet, poor land. Others: sweet potato and cassava (tropical lowlands), common and runner beans, squashes and pumpkins, tomato, chilli and sweet pepper, peanut, sunflower, pineapple, cacao, vanilla, plus tobacco, rubber and the fever-bark tree (cinchona). In 1490 none of these is in Europe; what must be brought is seed or tubers and the growers' knowledge of how to prepare them.
- Pitfalls: Bringing the plant without the preparation: maize as a staple without lime treatment causes pellagra, bitter cassava without processing poisons | Expecting instant acceptance; the potato took two centuries to become a field crop in Europe and was suspected as a poisonous nightshade | Looking for potatoes where Columbus landed; they grew in the Andes, first seen by Spaniards in the 1530s | Believing tomatoes, chillies or maize were always part of Italian, Indian or African cooking | Praising tobacco as a medicine, as 16th-century doctors did
- History: americas: c. 7000 BC – maize from teosinte (Balsas valley, Mexico); c. 8000–5000 BC potato around Lake Titicaca; squash, beans, cassava and sweet potato have separate domestication histories; europe: 1493 – Columbus brings maize and chilli; 1540s tomato and beans in Italy (Mattioli 1544); c. 1570 potato in Spain (Canary Islands 1567, Seville 1573); maize a field crop in northern Italy and the Balkans from the 16th–17th c., potato in the 18th c.; africa: 16th c. – maize and cassava brought by the Portuguese (cassava in Kongo by c. 1558); china: 16th c. – peanut, maize and (1590s, from Luzon) sweet potato; they feed the Qing population growth; india: 16th c. – chilli, then maize, potato and tobacco via the Portuguese; global: c. 1000–1200 AD – the sweet potato reaches Polynesia from South America before Columbus
- Read: Alfred W. Crosby, The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972) | Charles C. Mann, 1493: Uncovering the New World Columbus Created (2011) | Redcliffe N. Salaman, The History and Social Influence of the Potato (1949)

## Growing and storing potatoes `potato_cultivation`
- Core idea: To keep a variety true to type, propagate it from tubers: set whole small tubers or pieces with one or two eyes about 10 cm deep and 30 cm apart in rows 70 cm apart, after the last frost. As the shoots grow, draw earth up around them twice so that the new tubers form in the dark. Lift them when the tops have died down, dry them for a few hours and store them dark, cool and frost-free; keep the best for next year's planting. Do not grow them on the same ground more often than one year in three or four.
- Pitfalls: Eating the green parts: leaves, berries, sprouts and tubers turned green by light contain solanine and cause poisoning | Andean potatoes form tubers only when days are short; in the long European summer the first imports cropped late and poorly until adapted types were selected | Planting tubers saved from sick plants, which carries disease from year to year | Relying on one variety for a whole population (see potato blight) | Storing them in the light or where they freeze
- History: americas: c. 8000–5000 BC – domesticated in the Andes; freeze-dried chuño stored for years by the Inca state; europe: 1567 – shipped from the Canary Islands; 1573 bought by a Seville hospital; 1588 described by Clusius; 17th c. a field crop in Ireland; 1756 Frederick II's potato orders in Prussia; 1770s–1780s Parmentier promotes it in France; china: 17th c. – introduced, a hill crop by the 18th c.; india: early 17th c. – brought by the Portuguese
- Read: Redcliffe N. Salaman, The History and Social Influence of the Potato (1949) | John Reader, Propitious Esculent: The Potato in World History (2008)

## Maize, beans and squash grown together (milpa) `maize_beans_squash_milpa`
- Deps: helped by nixtamalisation, legumes_green_manure
- Core idea: A milpa is a maize field whose companion crops vary by community. In one maize–bean–squash system, sow maize in warm soil, four or five seeds to a mound, mounds a pace apart, in a block and not a single row because the wind must carry pollen from the tassels to the silks. When the maize is a hand high, sow climbing beans at its foot and squash between the mounds: the maize carries the beans, the beans fix nitrogen for their own growth and return some in their residues, the squash leaves shade out weeds and hold moisture. Eaten together, beans supply lysine, an amino acid in short supply in maize protein. Dry the ears well before storing; keep the best ears for seed.
- Pitfalls: Living on maize alone without lime treatment (pellagra) | Sowing in cold soil or a single long row; the seed rots or the ears set few grains | Damp storage: mouldy maize is poisonous | Expecting tropical varieties to ripen in a northern summer; quick 'flint' types are needed
- History: americas: c. 8000 BC squash (Guilá Naquitz, Oaxaca); c. 7000 BC maize in the Balsas region; common beans domesticated separately; the 'three sisters' reach eastern North America by c. 1000–1300 AD; europe: 1493 – maize seed brought by Columbus; 16th c. grown in Spain, Portugal and the Veneto, usually without beans or lime; africa: 16th c. – maize spreads along the coasts with Portuguese trade
- Read: Arturo Warman, Corn and Capitalism: How a Botanical Bastard Grew to Global Dominance (2003) | Charles C. Mann, 1491: New Revelations of the Americas Before Columbus (2005)

## Nixtamalisation (lime treatment of maize) `nixtamalisation`
- Deps: helped by lime_burning, vitamins_deficiency
- Core idea: Simmer dry maize kernels for half an hour to an hour in water with slaked lime (about 1 part lime to 100 parts maize by weight) or strong wood-ash lye, leave it to steep overnight, then wash and rub off the loosened skins and grind the kernels wet. The alkali frees the niacin that is locked up in maize, improves the protein and makes a dough that holds together. People whose diet is dominated by untreated maize and supplies little other niacin or tryptophan are at risk of pellagra: rough dark skin where the sun falls, diarrhoea, madness and death.
- Pitfalls: Bringing maize to Europe or Africa without this step, as actually happened; pellagra became endemic in some communities with monotonous maize-based diets | Using quicklime straight or far too much lime; it burns and makes the food inedible | Explaining pellagra as spoiled maize or an infection, the standard medical view until the 1910s | Skipping the wash; excess lime must be rinsed off
- History: americas: c. 1500–1200 BC – inferred from lime-soaking equipment on the Pacific coast of Guatemala; chemical traces only from Classic Maya sites; widely used by the Spanish arrival; 1937 Elvehjem and colleagues identify nicotinic acid through work on canine black tongue in the United States; europe: 1735 – Casal describes pellagra ('mal de la rosa') in Asturias; 18th–19th c. endemic in northern Italy; africa: 20th c. – pellagra outbreaks among maize-dependent populations
- Read: S. H. Katz, M. L. Hediger & L. A. Valleroy, Traditional Maize Processing Techniques in the New World, Science 184 (1974) | Daphne A. Roe, A Plague of Corn: The Social History of Pellagra (1973)

## Cassava and its detoxification `cassava_detoxification`
- Core idea: Cassava (manioc) is a tropical shrub grown from stem cuttings whose starchy roots yield heavily on poor soil, survive drought and keep in the ground for a year or two until needed. All varieties contain varying amounts of compounds that release prussic acid (cyanide). Traditional processing of high-cyanide roots combines several stages such as peeling, grating, fermenting, pressing and roasting. Breaking up the tissue allows the compounds to break down; liquid removal and heating help carry the cyanide away. The variety and the full process matter. Neither taste nor a fixed soaking time establishes safety.
- Pitfalls: Eating bitter cassava merely boiled, or shortening the processing in a famine: acute cyanide poisoning or lasting paralysis of the legs (konzo) | Assuming bitter and sweet kinds can be told apart by looking | Drinking the press liquid or reusing soaking water; both may contain cyanide | Living on cassava alone; it is almost pure starch with very little protein
- History: americas: c. 8000–6000 BC – domesticated on the south-western rim of Amazonia; staple of the Taíno, who gave Columbus cassava bread in 1492; africa: c. 1558 – introduced to Kongo by the Portuguese; spreads inland with the processing methods in the 17th–19th c.; india: 17th–19th c. – introduced to south India and Southeast Asia
- Read: William O. Jones, Manioc in Africa (1959) | Charles C. Mann, 1493: Uncovering the New World Columbus Created (2011)

## Potato blight and the risk of monoculture `potato_blight_monoculture_risk`
- Deps: needs potato_cultivation; helped by microorganisms, contagion_theory
- Core idea: A whole people living on one crop of one variety can lose everything in one season. Potato blight is caused by a water mould (an oomycete) whose spores blow from plant to plant in cool wet weather; leaves blacken within days and the tubers rot in the ground or in store. In Ireland in 1845–52, where many poor households depended on susceptible potatoes, particularly the Lumper, about a million died and more than a million emigrated. Defences: several crops and several varieties, healthy seed tubers, earthing up, cutting off the tops at the first black spots, and spraying the leaves before infection with Bordeaux mixture (1 kg copper sulphate and 1 kg slaked lime in 100 litres of water).
- Pitfalls: Blaming wet weather, bad air or 'degeneration' of the plant, as most experts did in 1845; the cause is a parasite | Spraying after the leaves are black; copper only protects healthy leaves | Treating the famine as a purely natural disaster; grain was exported from Ireland throughout and relief policy decided who died | Leaving diseased tubers and tops in heaps beside the field
- History: americas: origin in central Mexico or the Andes (disputed); 1843 outbreaks in the eastern United States; europe: 1845 – appears in Belgium in June, Ireland by September; 1846 M. J. Berkeley argues a fungus is the cause; 1861–63 de Bary proves it; 1882–85 Millardet's Bordeaux mixture
- Read: Cormac Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory (1999) | E. C. Large, The Advance of the Fungi (1940)

## The Columbian exchange (plants, animals and diseases across the Atlantic) `columbian_exchange`
- Deps: helped by new_world_crops, contagion_theory, variolation, quarantine
- Core idea: Sustained Atlantic traffic after 1492 carried American crops such as maize, potatoes and cassava eastwards. Wheat, sugar cane, livestock and European honey bees travelled westwards. Diseases crossed on different voyages: smallpox was recorded on Hispaniola in 1518 and in Mexico in 1520. Many communities had little prior immunity, and epidemics spread along existing networks, sometimes ahead of Europeans. Deaths varied greatly by region. War, displacement, enslavement and hunger compounded the losses.
- Pitfalls: Explaining the collapse of American populations by massacre alone, or by disease alone; epidemics struck peoples also hit by war, enslavement, forced labour and famine | Thinking the die-off was planned germ warfare; it was overwhelmingly unintended (deliberate cases are rare and late) | Assuming it can be prevented by good intentions; only keeping the sick ashore, quarantine and later inoculation reduce it | Stating as settled that syphilis came from America in 1493; the evidence favours it but is still debated | Releasing pigs, goats and rabbits on islands as a food store; they strip them bare
- History: americas: 1493 – Columbus's second voyage lands horses, cattle, pigs, wheat and sugar cane on Hispaniola; 1518–20 first smallpox epidemic from Hispaniola to Mexico; 1640s yellow fever arrives with the slave trade; europe: 1493 – maize; 1495 syphilis epidemic at the siege of Naples; 16th–18th c. American crops raise population; africa: 16th c. – maize and cassava; the plantation system drives the Atlantic slave trade (about 12.5 million people embarked, 1501–1867); china: 16th c. – maize, sweet potato and peanut open the hills to farming
- Read: Alfred W. Crosby, The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972) | Alfred W. Crosby, Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986) | Charles C. Mann, 1493: Uncovering the New World Columbus Created (2011)

## Food preservation (salting, drying, smoking, pickling) `food_preservation`
- Deps: helped by microorganisms
- Core idea: Food spoils because tiny living things grow in it; they need water, warmth and mild conditions. So take the water away (dry in sun and wind, or pack fish and meat in a quarter to a third of their weight of dry salt, or in brine of a measured strength appropriate to the food), make it sour (vinegar, or let shredded cabbage ferment under its own juice with 2 % salt to sauerkraut), smoke it after salting, boil fruit with its weight of sugar, or keep perishable food cold. Properly salted and dried fish and meat keep for a year or more; sauerkraut keeps through the winter and still protects against scurvy.
- Pitfalls: Too little salt, or meat sealed airtight without enough salt or acid: botulism, a deadly poison that cannot be seen or smelt (the name comes from sausage) | Smoking without first salting or drying; smoke alone does not preserve for long | Believing salt meat, biscuit and dried peas are a complete diet; they hold no vitamin C and crews get scurvy | Salting in warm weather before the meat has cooled, so that it rots from the bone outward
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – dried and salted fish and meat in ration lists; egypt: c. 2500 BC – salted and dried fish and fowl in tomb scenes; china: by Zhou–Han – fermented bean and fish pastes (jiang), salted vegetables; rome: c. 160 BC – Cato's recipe for salting hams; garum fish sauce an industry by the 1st c. AD; europe: from c. 1100 – stockfish trade from Lofoten; 14th c. Dutch barrel-cured herring; americas: pre-Columbian – freeze-dried potato (chuño) and dried llama meat (charqui) in the Andes; pemmican on the northern plains
- Read: Mark Kurlansky, Salt: A World History (2002) | Sue Shephard, Pickled, Potted and Canned: The Story of Food Preserving (2000)

## Canning (heat-preserving in sealed containers) `canning`
- Deps: needs food_preservation; helped by glassmaking, heat_sterilisation, microorganisms, safety_valve_boiler
- Core idea: Heat must reach the coldest part of the food for long enough, and a sound seal prevents contamination afterwards. Appert used corked bottles; modern preserving jars vent during processing and seal as they cool. A tested boiling-water process is suitable for sufficiently acidic foods. Tomatoes may need added acid even when they taste sour. Low-acid foods above pH 4.6, including meat, beans and most vegetables, need a tested pressure-canning process. Use the specified recipe, jar size, packing method, time and altitude adjustment; reaching a particular temperature alone is insufficient.
- Pitfalls: Boiling low-acid food (meat, beans, vegetables) at 100 °C only: the spores of botulism survive and the poison kills | Tasting suspect food: botulinum toxin can be present even when the jar is sealed and the food looks and smells normal | Large cans heated too briefly stay raw in the middle and rot (the Royal Navy scandal of 1852) | Sealing cans with lead solder on the inside | Appert's own explanation, that excluding air preserves; unheated sealed food spoils
- History: europe: c. 1795–1810 – Nicolas Appert develops bottling and wins the French government's 12,000 francs (1810); 1810 Peter Durand's English patent for tin canisters; 1812–13 Donkin and Hall's cannery supplies the Royal Navy; 1860s Pasteur explains why it works; americas: 1874 – pressure retort (Shriver, Baltimore); 1895–97 Prescott and Underwood work out safe heating times
- Read: Nicolas Appert, L'art de conserver, pendant plusieurs années, toutes les substances animales et végétales (1810) | Sue Shephard, Pickled, Potted and Canned: The Story of Food Preserving (2000) | US Department of Agriculture, Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015 revision)

## Pasteurisation `pasteurisation`
- Deps: helped by thermometer_temperature, microorganisms, fermentation_yeast
- Core idea: Gentle heating, well below boiling, kills most of the germs that spoil drinks or cause disease without changing the taste much. Wine and beer: 55–60 °C for a few minutes in the closed bottle or cask. Milk: 63 °C for 30 minutes, or 72 °C for 15 seconds, then cool quickly and keep clean and cool. Raw milk carries tuberculosis, brucellosis, typhoid and diphtheria; heating it sharply reduces infant deaths. Measure the temperature throughout the milk and time the hold from when the whole batch reaches it. Steam or bubbles alone cannot verify pasteurisation.
- Pitfalls: Thinking pasteurised means sterile; surviving germs grow again, so the milk still needs cold and clean vessels | Pouring heated milk back into the unwashed pail | Heating wine too hot, which spoils it | Believing milk sours because of thunder or bad air
- History: china: 1117 – the Beishan jiujing (Zhu Gong) describes heating sealed jars of wine to keep them; east_asia: by the 1560s – heating of sake (hi-ire) recorded in the Tamon-in diary, Nara; europe: 1768 Spallanzani shows heated sealed broths do not spoil; 1864–66 Pasteur heats wine; 1886 Soxhlet proposes heating milk for infants; from c. 1890 commercial milk pasteurisation (Denmark, Germany, New York)
- Read: Louis Pasteur, Études sur le vin (1866) | Patrice Debré, Louis Pasteur (1998)

## Grain storage and protection from pests and ergot `grain_storage_pest_control`
- Core idea: Grain keeps for years if it is dry (a kernel should crack between the teeth, not dent), cool, and shut away from rats, birds and weevils. Either store it airy in a granary raised on posts or stones with overhanging caps that rats cannot pass, and turn it; or the opposite, seal it airtight in a clay-lined pit or jar, where the grain uses up the air and insects suffocate. Clean out all old grain before the new harvest comes in. Rye with black, horn-shaped spurs among the grains carries ergot: segregate the lot. Visible sorting can reduce contamination but cannot certify its safety. Contaminated flour can cause burning pains, gangrene and convulsions.
- Pitfalls: Storing grain damp: it heats, moulds and can catch fire by itself; mouldy grain and nuts are poisonous even when they look only slightly spoiled | Climbing into a sealed pit or silo just opened; the air in it suffocates | Topping up an infested bin with the new harvest | Taking ergot poisoning (St Anthony's fire) for a plague or bewitchment | Open flames in a dusty mill or granary; flour dust in air explodes
- History: mesopotamia: c. 9000 BC – raised-floor granaries in the Levant (Dhra', Jordan) before full domestication; state granaries in Sumer; egypt: c. 5000 BC – basket-lined silos in the Fayum; later large state granaries; india: c. 2500 BC – large 'granaries' at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (identification disputed); china: 54 BC – 'ever-normal granary' (Geng Shouchang): the state buys grain in good years and sells in bad to steady prices; americas: 15th c. – Inca storehouses (qollqa) on windy hillsides, ventilated through floor channels; europe: Iron Age – sealed storage pits (tested at Butser); 1670s Thuillier and Dodart link ergot in rye to the disease
- Read: Peter J. Reynolds, Iron Age Farm: The Butser Experiment (1979) | Mary Kilbourne Matossian, Poisons of the Past: Molds, Epidemics, and History (1989)

## Sea fisheries – stockfish, salt cod and cured herring `sea_fisheries_salt_cod`
- Deps: needs food_preservation; helped by ship_design_caravel_carrack
- Core idea: Cod has almost no fat, so split, lightly salted and dried on racks or rocks it becomes hard as wood and keeps for years even in the tropics: the ideal food for ships, armies and fast days. In cold dry air (northern Norway, Iceland) it dries without any salt (stockfish). Fat fish such as herring must be gutted and packed in barrels of brine within a day of the catch. The richest cod grounds in the world are the shallow banks off Newfoundland, about 45–50°N and some 1,800 nautical miles west of Ireland.
- Pitfalls: Trying to air-dry fat fish; herring and mackerel turn rancid unless salted in brine or smoked | Drying cod in a warm, damp climate without enough salt | Asserting that Basque or Bristol fishermen worked the Newfoundland banks before 1492; there is no good evidence, though Bristol ships searched the western ocean from 1480 | Assuming the sea is inexhaustible; the Newfoundland cod stock collapsed in 1992
- History: europe: from c. 1100 – Lofoten stockfish traded through Bergen; 14th c. Dutch herring cure (attributed to Willem Beukelszoon, legendary); 1480–81 Bristol voyages in search of the 'Isle of Brasil'; 1497 John Cabot reports seas full of cod; from c. 1502 Portuguese, Norman, Breton and Basque boats fish off Newfoundland; americas: indigenous coastal fisheries for millennia; from the 16th c. salt cod feeds the Atlantic world; east_asia: dried and fermented fish products central to coastal diets since antiquity
- Read: Mark Kurlansky, Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World (1997) | Brian Fagan, Fish on Friday: Feasting, Fasting, and the Discovery of the New World (2006)

## Sugar from cane and from beet `sugar_cane_beet`
- Deps: helped by lime_burning
- Core idea: Sugar cane is a giant tropical grass grown from stem cuttings; its juice holds 10–15 % sugar. Crush the cane between rollers within a day of cutting, clear the juice with a little lime and skimming while heating, boil it down through a row of pans until it grains, and let the dark syrup (molasses) drain from the crystals in clay cones. The same sugar is in the white beet of temperate Europe: slice the roots, soak the sugar out in hot water, purify with lime and boil down. Selection raised beet from under 2 % sugar to over 15 %, so cold countries can make their own.
- Pitfalls: Cane cut and left lying for days loses its sugar; mill and field must work in step | Expecting cane to grow in Europe beyond the frost-free southern fringe (Sicily, Andalusia, Madeira) | Promoting cane plantations without seeing where they lead: they consumed forests for fuel and were the main engine of the Atlantic slave trade | Scorching the syrup or adding too much lime during clarification; crystals form when the syrup becomes supersaturated
- History: global: c. 8000 BC – cane domesticated in New Guinea; india: by c. 500 BC – cane juice boiled to solid sugar (Sanskrit sarkara); crystal sugar refined by the Gupta period (c. 350 AD); china: 647 – Tang Taizong sends a mission to India to learn sugar boiling; islamic: 7th–10th c. – cane and refining spread from Persia to Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus, Sicily and Spain; europe: 1420s–1450s – Portuguese plantations on Madeira; 1480s Canaries and São Tomé with enslaved labour; 1747 Marggraf finds sugar in beet; 1801–02 Achard's beet factory at Cunern, Silesia; 1811 Napoleon orders beet growing; americas: 1493 – Columbus brings cane to Hispaniola; first mills c. 1516; Brazil from the 1530s
- Read: Sidney W. Mintz, Sweetness and Power: The Place of Sugar in Modern History (1985) | J. H. Galloway, The Sugar Cane Industry: An Historical Geography from its Origins to 1914 (1989)

## Sericulture (silk raising) `sericulture`
- Deps: helped by textile_fibres
- Core idea: Silkworm eggs are kept cool over winter and hatched when the white mulberry comes into leaf. The caterpillars eat only fresh, dry mulberry leaves, on clean trays in a warm, airy room, for about four weeks and four moults, then spin cocoons on twigs or straw. Kill the pupae by steam or oven heat before the emerging moths soften and break through the cocoons, float the cocoons in nearly boiling water to soften the gum, catch the ends and reel five to eight filaments together onto a turning reel; one cocoon gives several hundred metres of unbroken thread. Let some moths emerge and lay eggs for next year.
- Pitfalls: Wet, dusty or wilted leaves and crowded, dirty trays: disease can kill the whole brood in days | Letting the adult moths emerge, which breaks the thread into short lengths fit only for spun silk | Starting with worms before the trees: mulberries need several years' growth, and about 200 kg of leaves go into a kilogram of raw silk | Assuming all mulberry foliage gives the same yield; white mulberry is widely preferred, but silkworms also eat other mulberry species | Breeding from sick moths (pébrine passes through the eggs)
- History: china: c. 3600–2700 BC – earliest silk finds (Qingtai, Qianshanyang); a state secret for millennia; india: c. 2450–2000 BC – wild silk in the Indus cities; mulberry silk later via Khotan; east_asia: by c. 3rd c. AD – sericulture in Korea and Japan; rome: c. 552 – silkworm eggs smuggled to Constantinople under Justinian (Procopius); islamic: 7th–10th c. – silk raising spreads from Persia and Syria to Sicily and al-Andalus; europe: 12th c. Sicily; 13th c. Lucca; water-powered silk-throwing mills at Bologna from the 14th c.; 15th c. Florence and Venice order mulberries planted; 1718–21 Lombe's mill at Derby; 1865–70 Pasteur shows how to select healthy eggs
- Read: Dieter Kuhn, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 9: Textile Technology: Spinning and Reeling (1988) | Luca Molà, The Silk Industry of Renaissance Venice (2000)

## Movable-frame beehive `beekeeping_movable_frame`
- Core idea: Bees keep open a passage of 6–9 mm (the 'bee space'): narrower gaps they glue shut, wider ones they fill with comb. Hang rectangular wooden frames in a box so that this working passage remains between the finished comb faces and between comb and box, and every comb can be lifted out, inspected and put back; honey is taken from an upper box and the colony lives on, instead of being killed with sulphur as in straw skeps. The simplest version is a trough covered by wooden bars 32–35 mm wide laid edge to edge, with sloping sides so the combs are not fixed to the walls. Smoke calms the bees.
- Pitfalls: Wrong spacing: frames get glued solid or bridged with wild comb and cannot be moved | Taking too much honey in autumn; a colony needs 15–20 kg to survive a northern winter | Calling the large bee the 'king'; she is a female, the mother of the hive | Moving combs between sick and healthy hives, which spreads foulbrood | Giving honey to infants under one year (botulism risk)
- History: egypt: c. 2400 BC – horizontal clay hives in the sun temple of Nyuserre; c. 900 BC a large apiary at Tel Rehov in the Levant; greece: 1682 – George Wheler publishes his account of Greek basket hives with movable top bars; continuity from antiquity is uncertain; china: by c. 2nd c. AD – the eastern honey bee kept in log and wall hives; americas: pre-Columbian – Maya keep stingless bees in log hives; 1622 European honey bee brought to Virginia; 1851 L. L. Langstroth applies the bee space (patent 1852); europe: 1609 Butler shows the 'king' is a queen; 1789–92 Huber's leaf hive; 1838 Dzierzon's movable bars; 1865 Hruschka's honey extractor
- Read: L. L. Langstroth, Langstroth on the Hive and the Honey-Bee: A Bee Keeper's Manual (1853) | Eva Crane, The World History of Beekeeping and Honey Hunting (1999)

## Coffee, tea and cacao `coffee_tea_cacao`
- Deps: helped by boiled_water, new_world_crops
- Core idea: Tea comes from Camellia sinensis. Heating the fresh leaves early limits oxidation and produces green tea; allowing bruised leaves to oxidise before drying produces black tea. Coffee uses the roasted seeds of a shrub native to the Ethiopian highlands. Cacao uses fermented, roasted and ground seeds of a tropical American tree; historical preparations included cold and frothed drinks. All three contain stimulants. Their preparation and trade differed: tea tolerated cooler growing conditions than cacao, and coffee houses and tea houses became meeting places for merchants and news.
- Pitfalls: Brewing unroasted coffee beans, or assuming tea and cacao require the same climate | Thinking green and black tea come from different plants | Repeating that Kolschitzky opened Vienna's first coffee house with beans left by the Turks in 1683; the first licence went to the Armenian Johannes Diodato in 1685 | In 1490 looking for coffee in Constantinople or cacao in Asia; coffee is then drunk only in Yemen and Ethiopia, cacao is already known in tropical South America as well as Mesoamerica
- History: china: tea drunk by the 1st c. BC (Wang Bao's contract, 59 BC); c. 760–780 Lu Yu's Classic of Tea; east_asia: 9th c. tea in Japan; 1191 Eisai reintroduces it with Zen; africa: coffee wild in south-west Ethiopia; chewed and brewed there before export; islamic: c. 1450 – Sufis in Yemen drink coffee to stay awake; 1511 debate and ban at Mecca; 1550s coffee houses in Constantinople; americas: c. 3300 BC – cacao used in the upper Amazon (Ecuador); by c. 1900 BC in Mesoamerica; cacao beans serve as money among the Aztecs; europe: 1520s–1544 cacao reaches Spain; 1610 tea shipped by the Dutch; c. 1645 coffee house in Venice, 1650 Oxford, 1652 London, 1685 Vienna
- Read: Ralph S. Hattox, Coffee and Coffeehouses: The Origins of a Social Beverage in the Medieval Near East (1985) | Sophie D. Coe & Michael D. Coe, The True History of Chocolate (1996) | Victor H. Mair & Erling Hoh, The True History of Tea (2009)

## Hybrid maize (hybrid vigour, seed bought anew each year) `hybrid_maize`
- Deps: needs selective_breeding; helped by heredity_genetics, mineral_fertiliser
- Core idea: Breeders cross selected inbred maize lines to produce a uniform first generation, often more vigorous than either parent. The gain depends on the cross and growing conditions. In the next generation traits segregate and average performance often falls. Seed producers therefore repeat the parental cross, preventing unwanted pollen from fertilising the seed-parent rows, and farmers obtain fresh seed for each crop instead of saving their own.
- Pitfalls: Saving and resowing seed from hybrid maize; the crop is uneven and yields drop | Overlooking shared susceptibility across varieties: in 1970 many US maize hybrids carried the same male-sterile cytoplasm, and southern corn leaf blight destroyed about 15 % of the crop | Confusing hybrids with the semi-dwarf wheats and rices, which are true-breeding varieties
- History: europe: 1760s – Kölreuter notes hybrid vigour in tobacco; 1876 Darwin's experiments on cross- and self-fertilisation; americas: 1908 – G. H. Shull describes inbred lines and hybrid vigour in maize; 1918 D. F. Jones's double cross makes seed cheap; 1930s–1940s hybrid maize covers the US corn belt; china: 1973 – hybrid rice (Yuan Longping)
- Read: Deborah Fitzgerald, The Business of Breeding: Hybrid Corn in Illinois, 1890–1940 (1990)

## Semi-dwarf wheat and rice (Green Revolution) `semi_dwarf_wheat_rice`
- Deps: needs selective_breeding; helped by heredity_genetics, mineral_fertiliser, ammonia_synthesis, irrigation_water_lifting
- Core idea: Semi-dwarf wheat and rice have shorter stems that resist lodging under heavy ears, especially with ample nitrogen and water. This is a different principle from hybrid maize: the varieties are stable, so farmers can save seed from them. Rust resistance was also important in the Mexican wheat programme.
- Pitfalls: Expecting the seed to work alone; without fertiliser and water the short varieties yield little more than the old ones | Calling the dwarf wheats hybrids; they are true-breeding varieties whose seed can be saved | Ignoring the side effects: falling water tables, salt, pesticide use and gains that go first to farmers with capital
- History: americas: 1944 – Borlaug starts wheat breeding in Mexico, semi-dwarf varieties released 1961–64; east_asia: 1935 – semi-dwarf wheat Norin 10 released in Japan (Gonjiro Inazuka); 1966 IRRI releases IR8 in the Philippines, bred from Indonesian Peta and Taiwanese Dee-geo-woo-gen; india: 1965–68 – Mexican dwarf wheats adopted in Punjab (Swaminathan); India self-sufficient in cereals by the 1970s
- Read: Norman E. Borlaug, The Green Revolution, Peace, and Humanity (Nobel Lecture, 1970) | Leon Hesser, The Man Who Fed the World (2006)
